body.p: We agree that direct experimental validation would strengthen the work. We have not added a new experimental dataset in this revision. Instead, we have made the experimentally testable status of the conclusions explicit. The revised discussion identifies total nuclear active Cyclin B–Cdk1 content and effective system size as controls of wave-back directionality, states that the nuclear enrichment required for complete reversal remains to be tested, and identifies perturbation of actomyosin contractility while monitoring Cdk1/Rho dynamics as one way to probe the role of omitted mechanics. We therefore present the work as a theoretical framework that generates concrete predictions, not as experimentally validated proof of the mechanism. See Discussion section in the revised manuscript.

disp-quote.p: (2) Adopts previously published models more or less 'as is', without detailed re-evaluation and re-assessment, or without developing them further.

body.p: We agree that the individual modules are adopted without substantial re-derivation or extension, and the revised manuscript now mentions this directly. We now discuss the models in the main text, mentioning the Yang and Ferrell / Puls Cdk1 model and the Michaud et al. cortical model, giving the equations and coupling, and then the Methods sections states that parameter values are retained from the original publications. Our aim is not to claim a new formulation of either module, but to analyze what emerges when they are coupled in a common geometry. That analysis yields the front–back asymmetry, geometry-dependent reversal of the Cdk1 wave back, and distinct cortical reactivation regimes. See Introduction, Model, Methods, and Results in the revised manuscript.

disp-quote.p: Overall, I find this work important, as it shows that combining models of the CDK1 gradient and Rho activation modules can explain the surface contraction waves observed in oocytes. Strikingly, it elegantly explains the differences seen between different experimental systems. While previously these were considered a 'controversy', modeling shows that the differences are simply a consequence of the difference in the size of the oocytes. In addition, the model makes several intriguing predictions that can be tested in future experiments.

body.p: We thank the reviewer. In revising the manuscript, we were careful not to reduce the mechanism to cell size alone: the model shows that directionality depends jointly on effective cell size and total nuclear Cdk1 content, which is set by nuclear size and nuclear concentration. We now mention this combination consistently and make the associated predictions explicit in the Discussion. See Results and Discussion in the revised manuscript.

disp-quote.p: Summary:

Using realistic mathematical models, Cebrián-Lacasa et al. address the relationship between waves of activation of Cyclin B-Cdk1 that propagate through the cytoplasm of large (~1 mm) oocytes and fertilized eggs and surface contraction waves (SCWs) driven by Rho GTPase activity in the cell cortex. They present numerical simulations of the underlying reaction-diffusion equations that account in broad strokes for both the expected behavior of 'fronts' of Cdk1 activation (that propagate at constant velocity from the nucleus-the source of Cdk1 activity-to the cell cortex) and the unusual behavior of 'backs' of Cdk1 inactivation (that may propagate either away from or towards the nucleus, or exhibit simultaneous inactivation throughout the cytoplasm). They also model Rho GTPase activity in the cortex as an excitable system that propagates SCWs (target patterns, spiral waves, and more complicated patterns). When Cdk1 is activated in the cortex, it phosphorylates and inhibits the RhoGEF, Ect1, which suppresses SCWs by reducing Rho GTPase activity. As the wave-back of Cdk1 inactivation moves across the cortex, Rho GTPase activity recovers abruptly, and SCWs reappear as 'phase waves' whose speed and directionality are determined by the underlying cytoplasmic Cdk1 signal.
Strengths:

As a theoretical examination of an interesting and puzzling aspect of early embryonic development, this study shares the same strengths and weaknesses as all mathematical and computational approaches to molecular cell biology. The mathematical models are precise formulations of the underlying assumptions of the authors (which are quite reasonable in this reviewer's opinion), and the analysis and computational results are dependable consequences of the molecular mechanisms the authors have in mind. The model is expertly analyzed, and the results are both reliable and intriguing. The results are discussed in light of experimental evidence. Because the authors' methods and results suggest novel-and sometimes counterintuitive-avenues for experimental research, this paper is likely to have a significant impact on the field of Rho GTPase signaling in oocytes and early embryos, and perhaps in other cells as well.

body.p: We thank the reviewer for this thoughtful assessment. We have preserved the mathematical formulations and made the assumptions, mechanisms, and experimentally testable consequences easier to identify. In particular, the revised Results section emphasizes the distinct mechanisms governing the activation front and wave back, the revised figures provide a more intuitive visual explanation, and the Discussion separates experimentally supported observations from model predictions. See Model, Results, and Discussion in the revised manuscript.

disp-quote.p: Weaknesses:

Like all mathematical models, the underlying assumptions can be critiqued as neglecting this -or-that 'crucial' effect (e.g., mechanical coupling via cortical tension or cytoplasmic flow, as the authors acknowledge), and the highly technical methods of analysis and simulation can be unfamiliar and off-putting to experimental cell biologists. The paper is a difficult read, even for an experienced theoretician. For those who take the time to understand this paper, it may change the way they think about the coupling of cell cycle control (Cdk1 activation and inactivation) and cell surface contraction waves.

body.p: We agree on both accessibility and model scope. To improve accessibility, we added the core equations and parameters to the main text, introduced more qualitative descriptions of the dynamical regimes, and redesigned Fig. 2B to show the physical mechanism schematically. We also expanded the discussion of the limitations. We did not add mechanical coupling to the model in this revision; instead, the manuscript now states explicitly that showing biochemical signaling to be sufficient within the model does not demonstrate that cortical tension, cytoplasmic flow, or surface deformation are unnecessary in living cells. These effects are identified as additional important factors that can affect the dynamics and as targets for future perturbation experiments. See Model, Results, Fig. 2B and caption (p. 6), Discussion in the revised manuscript.

disp-quote.p: (1) Carefully proofread the manuscript, Figures, and Figure Legends to make sure that statements are accurate. Please describe in more detail what is shown in every Figure panel. The units of diffusion in Figure 2C appear wrong, total activity is not really explained in the text, and it is a strange use, as the activity changes over time; the units of total activity are millimolar, which seems unrealistic. The Figure 1D heatmap does not explain what is plotted. Intensity is neither defined nor is it clear how the first wave front was drawn; the second appears to be convincing. The curvature of what physical object is plotted in Figure 1D, and again, how are the wavefronts on those Figures drawn?

body.p: We carefully reviewed the manuscript and all main and supplementary figures. Figure 1 was redesigned to show the model in 3D, 2D, and 1D and to make the coordinates used in the kymographs explicit. The revised Fig. 1 caption now states that the experimental color scales correspond to Cdk1-reporter intensity (top) and local membrane curvature (bottom), and that the dotted lines mark the tracked front and back. These overlays are intended as visual guides in the adapted experimental kymographs rather than quantitative fits used in our model analysis. Figure 2 was also redesigned and its caption expanded. The diffusion coefficient is now reported in μm2/s. In addition, we identified and corrected an error in the conversion of total active nuclear Cyclin B–Cdk1. The corrected control variable is total active nuclear content, reported in pmol and defined explicitly in Eq. 7; the affected main and supplementary plots were regenerated. See Fig. 1D and Fig. 1 caption (p. 3); Fig. 2 and caption (p. 6); Results, Methods, Eq. 7, Table 1 (p. 16) and Supplementary Figs. S3–S4 in the revised manuscript.

disp-quote.p: (2) Provide a better intuitive explanation of the proposed mechanism.

body.p: We substantially rewrote the Results section describing geometry-controlled directionality. The revised explanation first establishes the front–back asymmetry and then gives an intuitive description: a constant-speed activation front coexists with a slower diffusive spread of the elevated nuclear pool; because diffusion lags behind the front, distant regions can relax earlier, creating a gradient that drives an inward wave back. Revised Fig. 2B depicts these processes schematically. See Results, especially Fig. 2B and caption (p. 6) and Discussion in the revised manuscript.

disp-quote.p: (3) Reduce claims of novelty when not justified. I think that there is a potentially interesting idea in this paper, but also a lot of known facts that are revisited, and being unclear about what was known and what is new does not help the manuscript.

body.p: We agree. The revised Abstract and Introduction sections explicitly say that we couple established models rather than develop new individual modules. The Model section cites the original sources of each module, and the Introduction distinguishes established biological coupling from the question addressed here. We reserve the main contribution for the consequences of the coupled analysis: front–back asymmetry, the joint control by nuclear Cdk1 content and effective system size, and the resulting cortical response. The discussion also mentions the key unvalidated step as a testable prediction. See Abstract, Introduction, Model and Discussion in the revised manuscript.

disp-quote.p: (4) The interface of Cdk1 activity with actomyosin contractility (and cortical dynamics) is much better understood in other systems, and discussing those systems will improve the impact of the paper.

body.p: We expanded the Introduction to include Drosophila and zebrafish and to note the established functions of Cdk1-controlled actomyosin dynamics in nuclear positioning and ooplasmic segregation. This broader context makes clear that Cdk1–cortex coupling was already established and that our specific question is how cytoplasmic wave geometry shapes the downstream cortical response in large oocytes and eggs. See Introduction section in the revised manuscript.

disp-quote.p: (5) Be clearer about what the goal of this paper is and keep the focus on that. In my opinion, there is too much writing spent describing known facts.

body.p: We revised the Introduction to move more directly from the biological puzzle to the central question and then into the coupled model. The manuscript now explicitly states that we ask whether the opposite SCW directionality can follow from geometry and nuclear Cdk1 content rather than organism-specific cortical mechanisms, and then ask how the resulting cytoplasmic waveforms are transmitted to the cortex through Ect2 inhibition. We also reduced repeated background material and moved the core mathematical specification into a dedicated Model section. See Introduction, Model and Results in the revised manuscript.

disp-quote.p: (6) A discussion that the Cdk1 spatiotemporal patterns remain to be analyzed in both Xenopus and starfish embryos would be appropriate.

body.p: We added this limitation to the discussion in a way that distinguishes what is known from what remains to be measured. The revised text summarizes observations supporting nuclear enrichment and wave initiation but also says that whether nuclear active Cyclin B–Cdk1 reaches the levels required for complete wave-back reversal remains experimentally to be tested. We also avoid presenting the starfish intracellular Cdk1 wave as established fact. See Introduction, Results, and Discussion in the revised manuscript.

disp-quote.p: (1) I have one main suggestion. I would find it important that the authors present the models in more detail in the main text. In principle, even if they adopted previously published models, the reader should not need to go back to those original papers to find the equations and parameters. Readers should not even need to dig deep into the supplemental material. For example, the main equation used to model the CDK1 gradient should be shown in the main text with critical parameter values listed. For example, the text mentions that the diffusion coefficient of CDK1-Cyclin B has a critical importance (which I very much agree with), but I could not easily find the values used and still had to guess the units.

body.p: We agree. We added a dedicated model section to the main text containing the governing reaction-diffusion equations for both modules and the Cdk1–Ect2 coupling. The variables and roles of the principal parameters are defined there, while Table 1 lists the standard parameter values and units, including the diffusion coefficients used for the cytoplasmic regimes. The total active nuclear Cyclin B–Cdk1 control variable is defined explicitly in Eq. 7 in the Methods section. See Model, Methods, Table 1 (p. 16) and Eq. 7 in the revised manuscript.

disp-quote.p: (2) Overall, the manuscript is well written and nicely illustrated. However, the text could be more concise and, as explained above, show more equations rather than trying to describe them in words. Some of the illustrations could also be larger and possibly shown at higher contrast. Finally, the subtitles could be more imaginative, describing the main finding rather than simply stating what has been done.

body.p: We revised the manuscript throughout to reduce repeated background material and to replace lengthy verbal descriptions of the core model with equations in the main text. We standardized figure text and redesigned several panels, especially Figs. 1 and 2, to improve readability and interpretability. We did not replace every subsection title, but we have tried to use clear descriptive titles (with a message where possible). We revised several headings in the Results section so that they communicate the main finding directly, for example “Front–back asymmetry: traveling fronts and gradient-controlled backs,” “System size and diffusion modulate gradient effectiveness,” and “Phase diagram of Cdk1 waves.” See Introduction, Model, Results headings and text, Figs. 1– 2 and captions; supplementary figures in the revised manuscript.

disp-quote.p: (3) The starfish work focuses on meiosis I, not meiosis II.

body.p: We reviewed the stage-specific wording throughout. Rather than replacing every reference with “meiosis I,” we removed unnecessary stage labels where the argument concerns starfish oocyte meiosis more generally, and we use stage-specific wording only when it is supported by the cited experiment. In particular, Fig. 1 now labels the experimental panel simply as starfish meiosis rather than meiosis II. See Fig. 1D and caption (p. 3); Introduction and Results in the revised manuscript.

disp-quote.p: (1) Figure 1D. Right: experimental kymographs. What are 'intensity' and 'curvature'? I suppose 'intensity' refers to Cdk1 activity and 'curvature' to local curvature of the cell membrane. If so, Cdk1 activity seems to propagate as a wave around the cortex from the animal pole, but (I suppose) these are phase waves rather than trigger waves, because the nucleus is closer to the animal pole, so the cytoplasmic trigger waves reach the cortex sooner there and later at larger values of phi. In the starfish oocyte, the curvature 'bumps' at the animal pole and the equator seem to be stationary. Maybe I am misinterpreting the data; in any case, it might help readers to guide their reading of this data.

body.p: We clarified both the labels and the interpretation. The revised Fig. 1 caption explains the plotted experimental quantities as Cdk1-reporter intensity (top) and local membrane curvature (bottom), and mentions that the dotted lines mark the tracked front and back. We also distinguish the cytoplasmic propagation from the cortical phase-wave readout. Because the nucleus is off-center, the distance from the nuclear source to the cortex varies with angular position, so the radial Cdk1 solution is sampled at different times around the cortex. The Numerical methods now state explicitly that this geometry produces the angle-dependent arrival times shown in Fig. 1D. See Fig. 1D and Fig. 1 caption (p. 3); Model geometry and Numerical methods in the revised manuscript.

disp-quote.p: (2A) In panels (ii) and (iii), what is the meaning of the hyperbolic dotted line labelled 'underlying diffusion'?

body.p: The original schematic was replaced by the reworked Fig. 2B. The revised schematic and results now separate the outward trigger-wave-like front from the slower diffusive spread of the elevated nuclear pool. The “underlying diffusion” component is therefore no longer an unexplained fitted-looking curve; it is presented as the diffusive process that establishes the gradient controlling the wave back. See Fig. 2B and caption (p. 6) and Results in the revised manuscript.

disp-quote.p: (2B) This panel is very confusing. What is the significance of all the different colored lines? What is the meaning of '◄Time'? This panel needs more explanation. Also, fix 'increaseded'.

body.p: We agree that this was confusing. We now redrew Fig. 2B as a two-dimensional schematic with a consistent activity color scale and explicit labels for the phases and dynamical processes. The ambiguous time-arrow presentation was removed, and the typographical error was corrected. See Fig. 2B and caption (p. 6) and Results in the revised manuscript.

disp-quote.p: (2C) Units of diffusion constant are wrong; should be μm2/s. Also, please explain (perhaps in context of Figure S3) how you calculate 'units of active nuclear CycB-Cdk1 (mmol)' in terms of total [CycB-Cdk1] in the nucleus, radius of the nucleus, and model parameter γ.

body.p: The diffusion coefficient is now reported consistently in μm2/s. We also identified and corrected an error in the conversion to total nuclear amount. Eq. 7 now defines the total active nuclear Cyclin B–Cdk1 content from the enriched nuclear active concentration and nuclear volume; γ scales the nuclear concentration relative to the cytoplasmic baseline. The corrected quantity is reported in pmol, not mmol, and the corresponding main and supplementary plots were regenerated. Supplementary Fig. S3 shows that varying γ or nuclear radius collapses onto this single control variable. See Fig. 2D and caption (p. 6); Results, Methods, (Eq. 7), Table 1 (p. 16) and Supplementary Fig. S3 in the revised manuscript.

disp-quote.p: (2D) Please explicitly indicate the speed of the wave front, because it is difficult to read, given the scale of the vertical axis.

body.p: Agreed. The revised Fig. 2 caption now explicitly states that the wave-front velocities are fitted by a quasiconstant velocity of approximately 23 μm/min. See Fig. 2D caption (p. 6) and Results in the revised manuscript.

disp-quote.p: (3) Box 2. C. You might indicate that the Rho-actin dynamics are oscillatory for 0.59 < α < 1.02 and excitable for α slightly larger than 1.02 and (I suppose) slightly smaller than 0.59. Furthermore, I suppose (given the results in Figure 4) that the system does not propagate waves for α {less than or equal to} 0.5. Somehow, the authors should indicate how wave propagation is suppressed for small values of α.

body.p: We clarified the bifurcation structure and the low-α suppression of cortical activity. We did not adopt the proposed regime labels verbatim, because the spatial model supports propagating waves across a broader active window than the homogeneous oscillatory interval alone would suggest. The revised text therefore reports the two Hopf bifurcations at α = 0.59 and α = 1.02, states directly that the cortex is quiescent for low α, and reports that propagating waves persist across 0.59 < α < 1.26 up to the wave instability at α = 1.26. This directly explains how sufficiently strong Cdk1-mediated reduction of effective Ect2 suppresses propagation. See Box 2C (p. 9) and Results in the revised manuscript.

disp-quote.p: (4) Lines 273 and 294. "These differences arise...".

body.p: Corrected. The relevant Results text was rewritten during the broader restructuring, so the original wording no longer appears. See Revised Results.

disp-quote.p: (5) Lines 380, 381. "...the Hopf bifurcation (at α = 0.59) that separates...".

body.p: We did not retain the sentence in its original form. Instead, the revised text now identifies both Hopf bifurcations explicitly (α = 0.59 and α = 1.02), states the wave-propagating window, and then describes how Cdk1derived inhibition moves the cortical system across the bifurcation during suppression and recovery. We believe this is clearer than adding the parenthetical phrase to the old sentence. See Results and Box 2C (p. 9) in the revised manuscript.

disp-quote.p: (6) Table 1. Include a value for α_0.

body.p: Done. Table 1 now lists α0 = 1 (dimensionless), and the Methods state that α = α0 = 1 before nuclear envelope breakdown. See Table 1 (p. 16) and Methods in the revised manuscript.

disp-quote.p: (7) Line 522. What does 'implemented manually' mean?

body.p: We replaced the ambiguous wording. The Numerical methods now state that both models were integrated with an explicit second-order Runge–Kutta method implemented in custom code; the cytoplasmic and two dimensional cortical simulations use finite differences, and the three-dimensional cortical simulations use a finite element method implemented in FEniCSx. See Numerical methods in the revised manuscript.

disp-quote.p: (8) Figure S1. A. The first green dot should be labelled γ = 1. B. Left panel is γ = 1, I suppose.

body.p: Corrected. Revised Supplementary Fig. S1 explicitly labels the baseline γ = 1 condition and the enriched γ = 1.5 condition. Its caption also explains that γ scales the nuclear concentration above the cytoplasmic baseline while preserving the active-to-total ratio. See Supplementary Fig. S1 and caption; Model in the revised manuscript.

disp-quote.p: (9) Figure S2. What is X_0? How is it related to γ?

body.p: We addressed this by removing the X0 notation rather than adding another conversion. The revised supplementary analysis uses γ directly as the nuclear enrichment factor, defined in the main Model section and illustrated in Supplementary Fig. S1. The revised Supplementary Fig. S2 now focuses on the fitted wave-front and wave-back trajectories for different γ values. See Model, lines 123–132; Supplementary Figs. S1–S2; Methods, lines 620–638.

disp-quote.p: (10) References. Emphasis is on post-2010 literature. One classic paper on SCWs is mentioned: Hara (1971). The classic publication on Cdk1-driven mitotic waves in fruit fly embryos is Foe & Alberts (1983) J Cell Sci 61:31. The first theoretical prediction of Cdk1 trigger waves in syncytial cells was given by Novak & Tyson (1993) J Theor Biol 165:101. Citing Deneke et al. (2016) Dev Cell 38(4) could also be considered.

body.p: We added the suggested literature. Novak & Tyson (1993) is now cited for the early theoretical prediction of trigger-wave behavior; Foe & Alberts (1983) is cited in the discussion of cell-cycle/cortical waves; and Deneke et al. (2016) is cited in the Introduction both in the mitotic-wave context and in the broader discussion of Cdk1–actomyosin coupling. See Introduction and reference list in the revised manuscript.
